newsitem.title: LEBANON: Uproar in Lebanon over TV and radio closures.
newsitem.headline: Uproar in Lebanon over TV and radio closures.

text.p: Lebanese opposition leaders, religious figures and media workers on Thursday criticised as an assault on democracy a government decision to close about 200 television and radio stations.

They said the government was allowing political leaders to monopolise the media by licensing only 15 private television and radio stations owned by political leaders or businessmen and ordering the rest to shut down by November 30.
The stations slated for closure are barred in the meantime from broadcasting news.
"Where is the decency of the rulers, where is the shame of the rulers?" said former prime minister Selim el-Hoss in remarks published in newspapers on Thursday.

"Who will believe that the rulers' hegemony over the audiovisual media is not intentional to cancel the voice of the opposition from the media at the expense of general freedoms and democracy in this country?" Hoss wrote.
Around 100 media workers planned to stage a sit-in at the information ministry in Beirut on Thursday but policemen surrounding the building barred them from entering.
Newspaper reports said thousands would lose their jobs as a result of the government measure.

"The decision to divide the media among a number of top political leaders...is against the constitution and basic rules of democracy," a committee grouping media proprietors said in a statement on Wednesday night.

The government licensed the following television stations: Future Television of Hariri, NBN, a station which Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri is reported to be setting up, MTV of the brother of Deputy Prime Minister Michel al-Murr and Lebanon's top private station LBCI.

These stations, along with state-run television, are the only ones allowed to broadcast news. The government also licensed 11 private radio stations, allowing just three of the them to broadcast news.
Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri on Wednesday night denied the measure curbed freedoms.
"We proved through state television that all people get coverage and talk a lot against the government and the state," he told a delegation of Lebanon's Publishers' Syndicate.
The government argues that the measure closes one of the last chapters of the 1975-90 civil war. Some of the stations began as militia mouthpieces during the war but have since turned commercial.
The cuts also drew fire from religious leaders.

"Where is this government taking us...as it jumps over the constitution and the law to cancel the voices that express the people's will and which uncover the government's breaches?" said interim Druze religious leader Sheikh Bahjat Ghaith.
